reason: The sources provide over 15 claims supported across multiple independent sites regarding Phobos's discovery, physical characteristics, orbit, and predicted tidal destruction.
story: In 1877, astronomer Asaph Hall discovered Phobos, a tiny, potato-shaped moon orbiting Mars. Named after the Greek god of fear, Phobos holds a terrifying distinction: it orbits closer to its planet than any other known moon in the Solar System, just 6,000 kilometers above the Martian surface. Moving so fast that it completes an orbit in under eight hours, Phobos rises in the west and sets in the east twice every Martian day. But this close orbit is a death sentence. Gravitational tidal forces from Mars are relentlessly pulling Phobos inward by about two centimeters every year. Scientists calculate that in 30 to 50 million years, Mars will tear its own moon apart. The shattered, porous rubble pile will either crash violently into the Martian surface or break apart to form a dark, dusty ring around the Red Planet, completing Phobos's slow journey to destruction.
angle: Mars is relentlessly dragging its moon Phobos inward, doomed to tear it apart into a planetary ring or pull it into a fatal crash.

claims.claim: Phobos was discovered in 1877 by American astronomer Asaph Hall.
Phobos is the innermost and larger of Mars's two natural moons.
Phobos is named after the Greek god of fear and panic, a son of Ares (Mars).
Phobos orbits about 6,000 kilometers (3,700 miles) above the surface of Mars.
Phobos orbits closer to its primary planet than any other known natural moon in the Solar System.
Phobos completes an orbit around Mars in 7 hours and 39 minutes.
Because Phobos orbits faster than Mars rotates, it rises in the west and sets in the east as seen from Mars.
Phobos is an irregularly potato-shaped body with a mean radius of about 11 kilometers.
Phobos is more than seven times as massive as Mars's outer moon, Deimos.
Phobos is one of the least reflective bodies in the Solar System.
Surface temperatures on Phobos range from -4 °C (25 °F) on the sunlit side to -112 °C (-170 °F) on the shadowed side.
The dominant feature on Phobos's surface is a massive impact crater named Stickney.
Tidal forces from Mars are gradually drawing Phobos closer to the planet over time.
Phobos is predicted to eventually break up into a planetary ring or crash into Mars due to tidal forces.
Data from the Mars Express spacecraft revealed that Phobos contains large internal voids and high porosity.
The Soviet Phobos 2 spacecraft reached Mars in 1989 and collected data before suffering a fatal malfunction.
The Russian Fobos-Grunt mission carried the Planetary Society's LIFE experiment to test microbe survival in space.
The Russian Fobos-Grunt mission failed to leave Earth orbit after launch.
Phobos's surface exhibits distinct reddish and bluish regions.
Scientists debate whether Phobos is a captured asteroid or formed from planetary debris thrown up by an impact on Mars.

disputed: Timeframe until Phobos is destroyed: Sources vary between 30-50 million years, max 39 million years, or within 100 million years; script should state a range of 30 to 50 million years.
Origin of Phobos: Debated between captured C/D-type asteroid, impact ejecta from Mars, or disruption of a common parent moon body; script should frame this as an ongoing scientific debate.

Groove formation mechanism: Proposed theories include Stickney crater impact stress, rolling boulders from Stickney, or chains of impact ejecta from Mars; script should avoid stating one cause as absolute fact.
